lesson.title: Subordinate Clauses
lesson.subtitle: omdat, dat, als — the verb leaves second place and waits at the end

hook.title: The Verb Goes Home
hook.content: A main clause puts the finite verb second. A subordinate clause puts it last. Ik denk dat hij komt, ik werk omdat ik geld nodig heb. The conjunction sends the verb to the end.

pattern.title: Subordinating conjunction → verb final
pattern.content: After omdat, dat, als, wanneer and hoewel, the finite verb moves to the end of its clause. The main clause still has V2 order; only the subordinate clause changes.
pattern.linguist_note: Dutch is a V2 language in main clauses and verb-final in subordinate clauses, the same split German has.
pattern.trap_note: Want ('because') is different: it keeps main-clause V2 order. Omdat sends the verb to the end; want does not.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Subordinate Clauses):
exercises.target_answer: omdat, dat, als, komen, werken, denken
exercises.meaning: because, that (conjunction; relative), if, when, as, to come, to work, to think
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Subordinate Clauses": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “I think that he comes.”?
options: Ik denk dat hij komt niet.
exercises.explanation: “Ik denk dat hij komt.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Subordinate Clauses”.

exercises.idea: I work because I need money.
cues: The pattern: Subordinating conjunction → verb final
It means: I work because I need money.
idea_parts: I work because I need money.
exercises.target_answer: Ik werk omdat ik geld nodig heb.
exercises.meaning: I work because I need money.
exercises.explanation: “Ik werk omdat ik geld nodig heb.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Subordinating conjunction → verb final.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Want ('because') is different: it keeps main-clause V2 order. Omdat sends the verb to the end; want does not.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.german: Als het koud is, blijf ik thuis.
exercises.natural: If it is cold, I stay home.
options: If it cold is, stay I home.
If it is cold, I stay home.
not If it cold is, stay I home.
exercises.target_answer: If it cold is, stay I home.
exercises.meaning: If it is cold, I stay home.
exercises.explanation: “Als het koud is, blijf ik thuis.” is word-for-word “If it cold is, stay I home.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Subordinating conjunction → verb final.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: She says that we come.
exercises.explanation: “Zij zegt dat wij komen.” reuses only material taught in “Subordinate Clauses” — Subordinating conjunction → verb final.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Zij zegt dat wij komen.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Subordinating conjunction → verb final.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “I stay because it is raining.”
twist.explanation: Omdat sends the finite verb regent to the end of the subordinate clause.

summary.outcome: Put the finite verb last after a subordinating conjunction.
summary.takeaway: The conjunction is the signal: subordinate clause, verb final.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Verb-Final Gym.

omdat.context_phrase: Ik kom omdat ik tijd heb.
omdat.context_translation: I come because I have time.
omdat.etymology_derivation: A subordinating conjunction; the verb goes to the end.

dat.etymology_derivation: The neutral demonstrative and conjunction; also the het-relative pronoun.

als.context_phrase: Als het koud is, blijf ik thuis.
als.context_translation: If it is cold, I stay home.
als.etymology_derivation: English as and also are the same root; Dutch als covers if/when/as.

komen.etymology_derivation: English come and Dutch komen are the same verb; the vowel differs.

werken.etymology_derivation: English work and Dutch werken are the same verb.

denken.etymology_derivation: English think and Dutch denken are the same verb; th hardened to d.
